opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the things I find genuinely interesting. In the Mixtral paper, they looked at which experts the router was sending tokens to, and they were kind of hoping to see clean semantic specialization, like one expert handles biology, another handles math, another handles code. And they mostly didn't find that. When you broke it down by domain, the routing looked surprisingly uniform. What they did see was more syntactic or structural: certain experts would pick up on things like indentation in code, or particular tokens, or consecutive tokens tending to go to the same expert. So it's specialization, but not in the human-legible "this is the chemistry expert" sense.

Contrast that with some of the earlier mixture-of-experts work in vision, where people found much cleaner splits. You'd get experts that seemed to latch onto things like animals versus vehicles, or particular textures and object categories. It looked a lot more like what you'd naively expect.

How I interpret that: I don't think it means language models aren't specializing. I think it says our prior about what the natural units of specialization are is probably wrong for language. The model is carving up the problem in whatever way is most efficient for predicting the next token, and that doesn't have to line up with how we organize knowledge into university departments. A lot of what matters for prediction is local and structural, so it makes sense the router would pick up on that.

There's also a superposition angle here. Inside a dense model, features are smeared across lots of neurons, and you only recover clean, interpretable features when you use something like dictionary learning or sparse autoencoders. An expert in an MoE is a much coarser unit than a feature, so expecting each expert to be a clean concept is a bit like expecting a single neuron to be monosemantic. Sometimes you get lucky, as in vision, where the input space has more obvious natural clusters, but generally the meaningful structure lives at a finer grain.

So my takeaway is that routing analysis is a fairly blunt tool. If you want to know what the model has actually learned and how it's organized, you probably need to go below the expert level and look at features directly. I'd expect that once you do, you'd find plenty of domain-specific structure. It just isn't packaged neatly into experts.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the Mixtral evidence is actually really interesting precisely because it cuts against the intuition most people had going in. When the Mixtral paper came out, people went looking for the clean story: this expert handles code, this expert handles French, this one does math. And that's basically not what they found. When you look at the routing by domain, the experts get used fairly uniformly across ArXiv, GitHub, Wikipedia, whatever. The one place you see real structure is at the token level. There's syntactic specialization: certain experts tend to fire on indentation and whitespace in code, or on specific punctuation, or on consecutive tokens in a run. So it's less "expert for a topic" and more "expert for a kind of local token statistics."

And I think that makes a lot of sense when you think about what the router actually sees. It's looking at a residual stream vector at one position, and it's making a very cheap decision. The information that's most linearly available there, especially early in the network, is syntactic and positional stuff, not "we're now in a physics paper." Semantic specialization would require the model to have already done most of the work before routing, which is kind of backwards.

The vision contrast is interesting because vision models, and especially the earlier CNN interpretability work, did seem to give you more human-legible specialization. You get curve detectors, you get texture and edge detectors, you get the famous dog-face or wheel neurons. And there's a tempting read, which is that images have a more natural hierarchy of features and language doesn't. I don't think that's quite right, though. I think the difference is mostly about what you're measuring and where the pressure to specialize comes from.

In a dense vision model, a neuron specializes because it's the cheapest way to represent a reusable feature. In an MoE, the thing you're inspecting is the gating decision, which is being trained under a load-balancing loss that actively punishes you for sending all the physics tokens to one expert. So the training objective is literally fighting against clean domain specialization. If you removed the balancing term you'd probably get more legible experts, and also a much worse model, because you'd collapse down to using two or three of them.

So the way I'd put it is: the lack of semantic expert specialization in Mixtral isn't evidence that language models don't have specialized internal structure. The superposition and dictionary-learning results say they very clearly do. It's evidence that expert granularity is the wrong level to look for it. The specialization is happening inside the experts, distributed across features, and the router is doing something closer to a compute-allocation job than a knowledge-partitioning job. Vision models happened to put more of their legible structure at a level we could easily read off, but I'd bet the underlying picture is more similar than it looks.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between experts receiving different kinds of inputs and experts actually learning different capabilities. In Mixtral, the routing patterns don’t seem to support a clean story where one expert does mathematics and another does programming. You can see specialization around particular tokens or syntactic patterns, but that’s a weaker claim than semantic specialization.

In vision models, the evidence can look more intuitive: different experts receive different kinds of image patches, and sometimes those groupings correspond to recognizable visual categories. But even there, a routing visualization doesn’t establish that an expert has a distinct, indispensable capability.

The experiment I’d really want is to intervene: remove an expert or force inputs through a different one, and see whether a particular capability selectively deteriorates. So I’d read the evidence as stronger for interpretable specialization in vision, while being cautious about treating Mixtral’s experts as separate subject-matter specialists.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish an expert being used differently from an expert having a coherent specialty. In Mixtral, you can see differences in routing across tokens, but that doesn’t necessarily mean one expert does mathematics and another does French. The router might be picking up on relatively local features of the input, and the computation could still be distributed across several experts.

With vision models, it’s often easier to make the specialization visible: you can look at which images or patches activate an expert and see whether there’s a consistent pattern. That makes the evidence more interpretable, although a compelling visualization still isn’t a causal demonstration.

The test I’d really want is an intervention. If you remove an expert, do you selectively damage a particular capability, or does performance get a little worse everywhere? I’d put more weight on that than on giving experts names based on the tokens they happen to receive.
